brief.notification_title: Hot CPI pushes 10Y to 5%; tech and crypto slide
brief.market_summary: October CPI came in hot: headline +0.4% vs 0.3% expected, and core +0.3% vs 0.2%, the third straight 0.3%. The market now sees a December Fed hike as close to certain, and the odds of a 50bp move rose to about 15%. The 10Y is up 12bp to 4.99% and the 5Y up 16bp to 4.82%. The S&P 500 is down 0.73% at 7,495, giving back about a third of Monday's 2.35% rally. The Nasdaq is down 0.92%, and Nvidia is off about 5% on the Jensen Huang board probe. Brent is down 1.9% to $90.82 and briefly broke $90 as the Iran war premium keeps fading and OPEC output jumps. Crypto is leading the risk-off: BTC is down 2.1% at $73,462 and ETH down 4.7% at $2,034. All prices are intraday as of 11:21 ET. There is no close yet, and CoreWeave reports tonight.
brief.since_last: Yesterday's brief was written after an oil-driven relief rally. Today's CPI changed the rates picture. Core printed 0.3% against 0.2% expected, which meets the bar Waller had set for discussing a 50bp hike (n40, n147). Logan called for two more hikes, possibly in quick succession (n18). Yields rose most in the belly: 5Y +16bp, 10Y +12bp, 30Y +9bp. The dollar is up 0.66% and gold down 1.6%. Nvidia lost another ~5% as the probe into Huang widened to an alleged affair with a Chinese spy and congressional questions (n48, n145). Anthropic set its IPO range at $70–78, valuing it at up to $1.4T, with trading targeted for 19 Nov (n26, n119). Brent is about 23% below its 30 Oct high of $118. The OPEC survey shows Saudi output at 9.00M bpd vs 8.20M, Kuwait at 2.10M vs 1.77M and Iraq at 4.40M vs 4.10M. Crypto fell further: ETH is now just 1.7% above the $2,000 backstop in the ETH trim idea. Several items are still missing: the Tuesday close, CoreWeave's results, this morning's TDG/SE/ONON/VG results, and ETF flows for 9–10 Nov.

economic_data.takeaway: Headline beat, though it slowed from September. Energy was +0.7% and food +0.5%. No y/y figure was published because October 2025 prices weren't collected during the shutdown. Oil is down ~23% in two weeks, so the energy contribution should turn negative in November.

This is the print that matters: three straight 0.3% readings. December hike odds are ~84% for 25bp, and 50bp odds went from 0% to ~15%. That drove the belly-led selloff (5Y +16bp), a firmer dollar, and weakness in long-duration assets: tech, crypto and gold.
Expectations are stuck near 4%, which gives hawks like Logan cover. Lower gasoline (now under $4, n14) is the main hope for bringing this down.
Growth is not slowing enough to offset the inflation data. Together with 2.8% wholesale sales (vs 1.1% expected), it argues against any quick Fed pivot.
Firm nominal demand, partly reflecting September's higher prices. Minor for markets.

The yield is close to Monday's pre-CPI 2Y–5Y levels (4.56–4.67%), not today's ~4.75%. The timestamp looks garbled, so verify on TreasuryDirect before reading anything into demand. The 10Y and 30Y auctions are later this week; dates are unconfirmed.
Claims below 200K keep the labour market tight and support the hike case. A jump above ~220K would be the first argument for 25bp rather than 50bp.
This is the key risk for the IEF order. Core at 0.5% or higher would push 50bp toward the base case and the 10Y through 5%. An in-line print would let the CPI shock settle.
The next growth test before the FOMC minutes on 18 Nov and the 8–9 Dec meeting.

earnings.takeaway: Demand for power from data centres still shows up in reported profits even as sentiment on AI equities sours. The read-across is good for power producers, but XLU is down 0.7% today on higher yields. I have no price reaction for CEG.
Confirms CEG's message. Power producers are delivering the AI earnings that the chip stocks are now being asked to prove.

This is a September quarter earned at war-premium prices. Brent is now $90.82, down from $118 on 30 Oct, so Q4 numbers face a lower base. XLE is down 7.1% on the week, which shows the market is already looking past the beat.
Fits the financials leadership: XLF is +5.3% over the month and flat today despite the CPI selloff.

sections.summary: Hot core CPI and a 10Y near 5% reversed part of Monday's 2.35% oil-relief rally. The damage is concentrated in AI and semis: the Nasdaq-100 is about 10.6% below its 6 Oct record, while the Dow, financials and defensives hold up over the month. Nvidia's governance problems, CoreWeave tonight and the upcoming Anthropic IPO all weigh on the same stocks.
key_points: SMH −1.2% today, −7.1% on the week, −18.5% on the month. XLK −14% on the month. Nvidia −5% on the Huang probe and alleged spy affair (n48, n145).
Rotation, not capitulation: over the month XLV +8.7%, XLP +7.5%, XLF +5.3%, Dow +0.4%.
Anthropic IPO priced at $70–78 (up to $1.4T valuation), plus a $26B private placement, trading from 19 Nov. That is a lot of new AI stock competing for the same money.

sections.summary: The CPI beat repriced the Fed: a December hike is ~84% priced and 50bp odds are ~15%. Waller is open to 50bp and Logan wants two more hikes. The selloff is a bear flattener led by the 5Y. The 10Y sits just under 5%, which is where the IEF ladder starts filling.
key_points: IEF −0.90% to $90.97 and TLT −1.42%. LQD −0.94% vs HYG −0.50%: the losses come from duration, not credit stress.
3-month bill auction 4.060% and 6-month 4.145%. Cash in SGOV/bills now earns ~4.1% and will reset higher with each hike.
Over the month the 10Y is still −25bp, so this is a back-up after a strong rally, not a breakdown.

sections.summary: Brent is still unwinding its war premium. It touched $89.7–89.9, its first time below $90 since 31 Aug, after Trump said further Iran strikes are unnecessary and a return to war is 'highly unlikely'. Supply is rising quickly while Hormuz flows normalise. Today's stronger dollar adds to the pressure.
key_points: Brent at $90.82 (−1.9% today, −12.3% on the week), ~23% below the $118 high of 30 Oct. BNO at $58.16. WTI at $85.81.
OPEC survey: Saudi 9.00M bpd vs 8.20M, Kuwait 2.10M vs 1.77M, Iraq 4.40M vs 4.10M. LNG traffic through Hormuz is at a wartime high, and the US military is coordinating Saudi tanker crossings (n177).
Support: China's October crude imports hit 9.88M bpd, the highest since March (n172). Citi sees a $150 tail risk if Hormuz is disrupted again (n165).
Event risk: US-Ukraine-Russia talks in Abu Dhabi on 10–11 Nov (n94). The weekly API/EIA inventory reports have no confirmed dates.

sections.summary: Crypto is the weakest asset on the hot print: higher real yields and a firmer dollar on top of five weeks of selling. BTC is testing its 200-day average near $73K. ETH, SOL and XRP are falling 2–3x as fast as BTC. Corporate buying (Trump Media $112M) is being offset by miner selling (MARA sold 13,597 BTC).
key_points: BTC $73,462 (−2.1%, −11.8% on the month). ETH $2,034 (−4.7%, −11.4% on the week). SOL $82.36 (−5.4%). XRP $1.05 (−5.4%, −18.4% on the week). AVAX −7.0%. TON +6.5% is the lone outlier.

BTC ETFs lost $1.28B in the week to 6 Nov, the worst since June, and are now ~−$914M YTD. ETH ETFs lost $93M Friday and $99M Thursday. SOL ETFs have five straight weeks of outflows. 9–10 Nov flows not available.
MARA sold $1.1B of BTC to repay loans and plans more sales (n33), even while announcing a $500M buyback (n10). ~$360M of liquidations after CPI (n63).
ETH-specific drags: the Glamsterdam testnet delay over gas-accounting risks, and a narrative shift as Vitalik recasts ETH as a store of value (n156).

brief.instructor_take: Here's what I'd focus on today. The headline number matters less than the third straight 0.3% core print. That turns December from 'maybe' into 'how big', and you can see it in the curve: the 5Y rose 16bp while the 30Y rose 9bp. The crowd reads that as 'sell everything', but look underneath. The Dow is up on the month, financials and health care are leading, and HYG fell half as much as LQD. This is a rotation out of long-duration growth and AI, not a credit event. The AI complex also has its own problems on top of rates: a CEO governance scandal at Nvidia, CoreWeave's debt load tested tonight, and a $1.4T Anthropic IPO that will draw money from the same holders on 19 Nov. Meanwhile the biggest disinflation force of the quarter is happening in plain sight: Brent is down 23% in two weeks and gasoline is under $4. The Fed is looking at core, not oil, so that won't help December, but it should cap how far 10Y yields run in the months after. So I stay underweight semis, let the IEF ladder fill near 5%, keep cash in bills at ~4.1%, and stay out of falling assets like oil and altcoins. A less experienced investor might chase Monday's 2.35% rally or buy XRP below a dollar. One relief day doesn't reverse a trend in which SMH is down 18% in a month. What would change my mind is a soft PPI on Friday combined with a strong AMAT on Thursday. Then I'd start rebuilding tech.

top_ideas.title: Stay out of semis until AMAT and Nvidia report
top_ideas.one_liner: Semis still broken: no buying before AMAT and Nvidia
top_ideas.thesis: Semis are in a correction for several reasons: higher real yields, Nvidia governance risk, scrutiny of AI debt and a large AI IPO coming. Major catalysts land over the next nine days. Yesterday's re-entry condition (core CPI 0.2% or lower) failed, so the position stays trimmed.
top_ideas.reasoning: I start with the evidence. SMH is down 18.5% in a month and 7.1% in a week, and it fell again today even after Monday's broad 2.35% rally, which Nvidia also missed. When a sector can't join a relief rally, that's distribution, not a dip. The rates channel works against it too. A 0.3% core print pushes up the discount rate on long-duration growth, and the 10Y near 5% is the competing return. Then there are the sector's own problems: the Huang probe has reached Congress (n145), CoreWeave tonight tests whether debt-funded AI capex holds up (n51), and the Anthropic IPO brings up to $1.4T of new AI stock on 19 Nov. I prefer avoiding SMH over shorting anything because the investor is long-only, and holding off costs only ~4% a year in forgone bill yield. The thing beginners miss is that waiting for confirmation costs a few percent of upside but avoids the -20% path. I'd change my mind if AMAT beats and guides up and SMH closes above $508, about 5.5% above here, which would show buyers absorbing the bad news.

top_ideas.entry: No new buying. Hold tech and semis at the trimmed weight and keep the proceeds in SGOV. Re-entry rule: if SMH closes above ~$508 after AMAT beats and guides up, rebuy half at the next open and half after the first down day. If Nvidia disappoints on 17 Nov, wait.
top_ideas.invalidation: SMH closes above ~$508 after an AMAT beat-and-raise and holds it through Nvidia on 17 Nov. Then I rebuild the trimmed position.
top_ideas.sizing: 0% new exposure. Keep semis/tech at the already-trimmed weight and the cash in SGOV.

top_ideas.title: Finish the IEF ladder near a 5% 10-year
top_ideas.one_liner: 10Y near 5%: hold IEF half, keep $90.60 bid through Friday
top_ideas.thesis: The CPI back-up filled the first half of the IEF ladder at ~$91.20. With the 10Y at 4.99%, the hike shock is landing mostly on the 5Y. Collapsing oil and an equity correction argue for owning intermediate duration on this weakness, but only up to the planned size until PPI is out.
top_ideas.reasoning: The logic runs like this. A third 0.3% core print means the Fed hikes in December, but 84% of that is already priced, and the move today was a bear flattener: the 5Y rose 16bp and the 10Y 12bp. The market is putting the hikes into the front and belly, not demanding much more term premium. Looking a few months ahead, Brent is down 23% in two weeks and gasoline is under $4. That will pull headline inflation and eventually inflation expectations (3.9%) lower, which favours the 10Y once the Fed is done. I choose IEF over TLT because the 30Y auction is this week and the long end carries more supply risk. I choose it over SHY because the front end takes the full hit if 50bp becomes the base case. A 10Y near 5% also pays well while I wait, and it hedges the equity correction if growth stocks keep sliding. Today Waller is open to 50bp and Logan wants two more hikes, so the Fed-signal half of my invalidation is being tested, which is why I won't add beyond the second tranche. If core PPI prints 0.5% or more, or 50bp becomes the majority view, I stop buying and reassess.

risks: Hot PPI pushes December odds toward 50bp
Weak 10Y/30Y auctions on top of rising deficits

GDPNow at 3.5% means growth isn't helping the bond case
top_ideas.entry: First half filled at ~$91.20; IEF is now $90.97. Keep the second-half GTC limit at ~$90.60 (≈5.04% 10Y) through Fri 13 Nov, funded from SGOV. No adds beyond the two tranches. Cancel the unfilled half if PPI core is 0.5% or higher before it fills.
top_ideas.invalidation: The 10Y closes above 5.20% (IEF ~$89.6), or futures price a 50bp December hike as more likely than not. Either means the hike cycle is bigger than one gradual 25bp step.
top_ideas.sizing: Total position 3–5% of the portfolio across both halves, unchanged from the plan.

top_ideas.title: Trim a third of ETH; lower the sell limits
top_ideas.one_liner: ETH at $2,034: trim a third, $2,000 close is the backstop
top_ideas.thesis: ETH is the high-beta loser in a tighter-money tape: it fell 4.7% vs BTC's 2.1% today, with ETF outflows and upgrade delays. Yesterday's $2,250/$2,300 limits are now 10–13% away, so I bring them closer and keep the $2,000 daily-close backstop.
top_ideas.reasoning: I start with relative strength, because a trim should come from the weakest holding. ETH is down 11.4% on the week vs BTC's 5.2%, and down 19% on the month. A firmer dollar and higher real yields hurt non-yielding assets, and ETH has been the most sensitive of the large ones. Flows confirm it: two straight days of ETH ETF outflows ($99M, then $93M), with BTC ETFs negative for the year. ETH also has its own drags: the Glamsterdam testnet delay over contract-breaking gas changes, and a shift in its narrative that unsettles holders (n156). I trim ETH rather than BTC because BTC still has corporate buyers like Trump Media and is testing a level the market watches, its 200-day average. ETH has neither support. I use limits slightly above the market instead of selling at market because $2,000 is an obvious round number where reflex bounces happen, and the backstop covers me if the bounce doesn't come. The mistake to avoid is cutting the whole position at the low. This is one-third, to reduce risk, not a bet on zero. I'd change my mind if ETH reclaims $2,400 with three straight days of ETF inflows.
catalysts: Daily ETF flow prints for 9–10 Nov onward
risks: Short squeeze from the $2,000 area triggers the limits only after the rally
A soft PPI or dovish Fed talk lifts all risk assets
top_ideas.entry: Cancel the $2,250/$2,300 GTC sells. Replace them with GTC limit sells for one-third of ETH (spot or ETHA): half at $2,150 and half at $2,200, good through Fri 20 Nov. Backstop: if ETH has a daily close below $2,000 before they fill, sell the unfilled part the next day. Proceeds go to SGOV.
top_ideas.invalidation: ETH closes above $2,400 and spot ETH ETFs post three straight sessions of inflows. Cancel any unfilled sells.
top_ideas.sizing: Sell one-third of existing ETH exposure. No new crypto buying.

brief.prior_ideas_review: 1) BUY IEF: the CPI back-up did what we waited for. IEF fell from ~$91.80 to $90.97, so the first half filled at ~$91.20 and is down ~0.25%. The second half at $90.60 hasn't filled, and the 10Y at 4.99% is well below the 5.20% invalidation. Waller's openness to 50bp and Logan's call for two hikes partly test the 'Fed signals more than one gradual 25bp' condition. Keep the position, keep the $90.60 order through Friday's PPI, and add nothing beyond it. 2) AVOID SMH: this worked. SMH is down another 1.2% to $481.74 (−7.1% on the week). The re-entry condition required core CPI at 0.2% or lower, and it printed 0.3%. Keep it, with the trigger now tied to AMAT and Nvidia on 17 Nov. 3) TRIM ETH: not filled. ETH went the other way, from ~$2,134 to $2,034, nowhere near the $2,250/$2,300 limits. It is now 1.7% above the $2,000 close backstop. The thesis is stronger, so keep the idea but move the limits down to $2,150/$2,200.

lesson.explanation: A bear flattener is when yields rise across the curve ('bear', because bond prices fall) but short and intermediate yields rise more than long ones, so the curve gets flatter. It usually happens when the market expects the central bank to hike: the front end prices the hikes directly, while the long end expects tighter policy now to slow growth and inflation later. In a bear flattener, intermediate bonds are often a better place to add duration than the very short end, which takes the full hike repricing. The ultra-long end brings its own supply and term-premium risks.
lesson.todays_example: After the 0.3% core CPI, the 5Y rose 16.2bp, the 10Y 12.3bp and the 30Y only 9.4bp. That is why the IEF idea uses the 7–10Y bucket, why SHY fell 0.34% despite its short maturity, and why TLT's bigger drop (−1.42%) reflects duration, not the long end leading the move.
